pharm: 8-aminoquinoline that, through CYP2D6-generated hydroxylated metabolites and oxidative stress, kills dormant hepatic hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax to achieve radical cure and prevent relapse
tags: G6PD DEFICIENCY: risk of severe/fatal hemolytic anemia
quick: 15 mg base (26.3 mg phosphate, 1 tablet) once daily for 14 days
With or without food; food may reduce GI upset
Contraindicated - risk of hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient fetus
Contraindicated if infant is G6PD deficient or G6PD status unknown
No specific adjustment; data limited - monitor
No specific adjustment; data limited - monitor

summary: Primaquine is an 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial used for the radical cure (prevention of relapse) of vivax malaria by eradicating the dormant liver-stage hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax. It is given to adults concurrently with or after chloroquine, which clears the blood-stage parasites. The central safety issue is hemolytic anemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)-deficient individuals, which can be severe or fatal: G6PD testing must be performed before use, and primaquine is contraindicated in severe G6PD deficiency. It is also contraindicated in pregnancy (the fetus may be G6PD deficient even if the mother is not), in breastfeeding when the infant is G6PD deficient or of unknown G6PD status, and with quinacrine. Additional cautions include methemoglobinemia, leukopenia, and QT-interval prolongation.
indications: Radical cure (prevention of relapse) of vivax malaria, including following termination of chloroquine suppressive therapy in areas where vivax malaria is endemic

dosage.r: Radical cure / prevention of relapse of P. vivax malaria
dosage.d: 1 tablet (26.3 mg phosphate = 15 mg base) once daily
dosage.n: Give concurrently with a course of chloroquine phosphate, which clears the erythrocytic (blood-stage) parasites; may take with or without food

admin: Perform G6PD testing BEFORE administering primaquine
Obtain baseline hemoglobin and hematocrit before treatment; postpone testing and treatment decision in severe anemia until recovery
Give concurrently with chloroquine phosphate to first destroy the blood-stage parasites
Take with or without food; taking with food may reduce gastrointestinal symptoms
Pregnancy test sexually active females of reproductive potential before starting
Dosing is customarily expressed in terms of the base (15 mg base = 26.3 mg phosphate)
moa: Primaquine is an 8-aminoquinoline whose mechanism is not fully established but is thought to involve inhibition of the mitochondrial system of dormant parasites and oxidative stress generated by reactive metabolites in infected cells. Its activity is probably related to hydroxylated metabolites generated in the liver by CYP2D6. It is active against the dormant liver forms (hypnozoites) and exoerythrocytic stages of P. vivax, thereby preventing the blood-stage forms responsible for relapse, and is also active against gametocytes of P. falciparum.

absolute: Severe G6PD deficiency - risk of severe or fatal hemolytic anemia
Pregnancy - may cause hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient fetus (fetus may be G6PD deficient even if mother is not)
Breastfeeding when the infant is G6PD deficient or the infant's G6PD status is unknown
Concurrent use of quinacrine, or recent prior quinacrine (increased toxicity)
Known hypersensitivity to primaquine, other 8-aminoquinolines, or any component
relative: Mild to moderate G6PD deficiency - only after individual risk-benefit assessment with close hematologic monitoring
Unknown G6PD status when testing unavailable - only after risk-benefit assessment with monitoring
NADH methemoglobin reductase deficiency or concurrent methemoglobinemia-inducing drugs (e.g. dapsone, sulfonamides)
Pre-existing granulocytopenia (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) - risk of leukopenia
Cardiac disease, long QT syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia history, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, or QT-prolonging drugs
CYP2D6 poor/intermediate metabolizers or potent CYP2D6 inhibitors - higher treatment-failure (relapse) risk
monitor: G6PD status must be tested before use
Baseline and on-treatment hemoglobin/hematocrit (e.g. day 3 and day 8) where hemolytic risk exists
Leukocyte count; ECG in patients at QT risk

preg: Primaquine is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Safe use in pregnancy has not been established, and primaquine may cause hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient fetus - importantly, the fetus may be G6PD deficient even when the mother has normal G6PD levels. Nonclinical data show gene mutations, chromosomal/DNA damage, teratogenicity (including cleft palate and small chin in rats), and embryo-fetal injury. Sexually active females of reproductive potential should have a pregnancy test before starting and use effective contraception during treatment and until 2 menses have elapsed; treated males with partners who may become pregnant should use a condom during treatment and for 3 months afterward.
lact: Primaquine is contraindicated in breastfeeding women when the infant is found to be G6PD deficient or the infant's G6PD status is unknown, because a G6PD-deficient breastfed infant is at risk of hemolytic anemia. Infant G6PD status should be checked before breastfeeding begins. In a study of 21 G6PD-normal lactating women and their G6PD-normal infants given a 0.5 mg/kg/day base dose for 14 days, the estimated infant ingested dose was less than 1% of the maternal dose and infant plasma concentrations were largely below measurement thresholds. There is no information on effects on the breastfed infant or on milk production.
renal: The efficacy and safety of primaquine after repeated dosing have not been assessed in renal impairment, and there is no specific dosing adjustment because of limited data. Single-dose studies in severe (eGFR 15-29 mL/min) or end-stage (<15 mL/min) renal impairment showed up to ~1.7-fold higher primaquine Cmax but no major difference in AUC or half-life. If used, monitor efficacy and for adverse reactions, particularly in severe renal impairment.
hepatic: The efficacy and safety of primaquine after repeated dosing have not been assessed in hepatic impairment, and there is no specific dosing adjustment because of limited data. A single-dose study showed about a 3-fold lower primaquine Cmax in moderate hepatic dysfunction without significant AUC change. Because primaquine is metabolized in the liver to active metabolites, effects on efficacy are uncertain; if used, monitor efficacy and for adverse reactions, particularly in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Hemolytic agents - avoid concurrent use; additive hemolysis risk
Methemoglobinemia-inducing drugs (e.g. dapsone, sulfonamides) - risk of severe methemoglobinemia
moderate: QT-prolonging drugs - additive QT risk; close, frequent ECG monitoring advised
Potent CYP2D6 inhibitors - may reduce active metabolite formation and antimalarial efficacy; increase relapse monitoring or use alternatives
Bone-marrow depressants - avoid concurrent use (leukopenia risk)
minor: CYP1A2 substrates (e.g. duloxetine, alosetron, theophylline, tizanidine) - primaquine may increase their exposure; monitor
Narrow-therapeutic-index P-gp substrates (e.g. digoxin, dabigatran) - primaquine may increase their concentrations; monitor
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food may reduce gastrointestinal symptoms (a high-fat meal modestly raised exposure ~14% AUC and ~26% Cmax)
interactions.diagnostics: G6PD testing must precede therapy; obtain baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit and monitor blood counts and methemoglobin in at-risk patients

common: Nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, abdominal cramps
serious: Hemolytic anemia - occurs commonly in G6PD deficiency and may be severe or fatal in severe G6PD deficiency
Severe methemoglobinemia (especially with NADH methemoglobin reductase deficiency or methemoglobinemia-inducing drugs)
Leukopenia (notably in patients with established granulocytopenia such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus)
emergency: Acute severe hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients (dark urine, pallor, shortness of breath, dizziness, fatigue) - stop drug and seek care immediately
Severe methemoglobinemia (bluish lips or nails, cyanosis)
Serious cardiac arrhythmia / marked QT prolongation

monitoring: G6PD testing MUST be performed before initiating primaquine
Baseline hemoglobin and hematocrit; close hematologic monitoring (e.g. day 3 and day 8) when any hemolytic risk exists
Signs of hemolysis - darkening of urine, pallor, shortness of breath, dizziness, fatigue
Methemoglobin levels in at-risk patients; watch for bluish lips or nails
Leukocyte count - discontinue promptly for a sudden decrease
ECG in patients with cardiac disease, QT-risk factors, or on QT-prolonging drugs
Pregnancy test before treatment in females of reproductive potential
counsel: You must be tested for G6PD deficiency before taking this medicine
Stop the drug and contact your provider immediately if your urine darkens or you develop paleness, shortness of breath, dizziness, or unusual tiredness (signs of red-cell breakdown)
Seek immediate care if your lips or nails turn bluish (a sign of methemoglobinemia)
Take one tablet once daily for 14 days, with or without food; food may ease stomach upset
Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant; use effective contraception during treatment and until 2 menstrual periods have passed (men: use a condom during and for 3 months after treatment)
Tell your provider about all other medicines, especially quinacrine, dapsone, sulfonamides, and any heart-rhythm or QT-affecting drugs
pk: Rapidly absorbed; Tmax about 2.3 hours after an oral dose
At 15 mg base once daily, primaquine Cmax about 50 ng/mL
Mean terminal half-life about 5.6 hours (active metabolite carboxyprimaquine ~22 hours)
Once-daily dosing over a 14-day course; little accumulation of primaquine across days 1-14
Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions 15-30 C; dispense in a tight, light-resistant container
pearls: G6PD deficiency is the central safety issue - test G6PD BEFORE use; hemolytic anemia can be severe or fatal in severe G6PD deficiency
Contraindicated in severe G6PD deficiency, in pregnancy (fetus may be G6PD deficient even if mother is normal), and with quinacrine
Kills dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax (radical cure) - give with chloroquine, which clears the blood-stage parasites
Watch for methemoglobinemia (bluish lips/nails) - worse with NADH methemoglobin reductase deficiency or dapsone/sulfonamides
Efficacy depends on CYP2D6 activation - poor/intermediate metabolizers or CYP2D6 inhibitors have higher relapse (treatment-failure) rates
Caution with QT prolongation; also active against P. falciparum gametocytes (transmission blocking)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your once-daily schedule. Do not take two tablets at once. Complete the full 14-day course, and tell your provider about any missed doses since incomplete treatment can allow relapse.
overdose: Symptoms of overdose include abdominal cramps, vomiting, burning epigastric distress, CNS effects (headache, insomnia), cardiovascular effects including cardiac arrhythmia and QT prolongation, methemoglobinemia (cyanosis), leukocytosis or leukopenia, granulocytopenia, and anemia. Acute hemolysis can be especially severe in G6PD-deficient patients. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive; consider contacting a poison center or medical toxicologist for management guidance.
